title: Why I Founded CatchDog
excerpt: CatchDog started as a workflow automation idea. But building a company with generative AI at its core quickly changed the scope of what was possible.
body:
When I started building CatchDog LLC, the initial idea was very specific: help small and mid-sized businesses automate workflows and connect the tools they already use.

But something became clear very quickly. A company born with generative AI at its core does not remain limited to one category of service. As the technology evolves, the scope of what can be built also expands.

That is why CatchDog LLC gradually became more than a workflow automation project. Today, the work can include functional systems, lightweight interfaces, dashboards, SaaS-style prototypes, operational automations, audiovisual content, explainers, and AI-assisted problem solving. Not because the goal is to “do everything,” but because many business problems do not fit neatly into one technical box.

Most SMBs do not need a massive software implementation. They need someone who can understand the problem, translate it into a practical digital solution, and deliver something usable without turning the process into a long and expensive enterprise project.

This is the logic behind CatchDog LLC: use AI not as a gimmick, but as a working layer that helps move faster across strategy, systems, interfaces, content, and execution.

I do not think clients always need to know every tool or technical step behind the solution. What they need is clarity, functionality, and results they can actually use.

That is the kind of company I wanted to build: small, flexible, AI-native, and focused on solving real operational problems with lightweight technology.

title: The Operating Nervous System: How AI Agents Are Rewiring Business Operations
excerpt: Organizations are hitting the same wall: fragmented tools, repetitive tasks, and communication flows that nobody designed — they just accumulated.
body:
CatchDog was born from a simple premise: most small and mid-sized businesses do not need heavy enterprise software. They need practical digital systems that solve real operational problems. At first, that meant workflow automation and tool integration. But a company built natively with generative AI does not stay confined to one narrow category. As the technology evolves, so does the range of problems it can address.

That is why CatchDog is not just an “automation company.” It builds end-to-end functional systems, interfaces, control panels, lightweight dashboards, SaaS-style prototypes, audiovisual assets, scripts, explainers, and AI-assisted operational solutions. The client does not need to know every tool, API, model, platform, or technical layer behind the result. What matters is that the problem is understood, translated into a usable system, and delivered in a way the business can actually operate.

This is the real shift: generative AI allows a small, flexible team to cover areas that used to require separate specialists, agencies, developers, designers, content producers, and consultants. CatchDog can move from diagnosing a workflow problem to building a prototype, creating a front-end interface, designing supporting content, and automating repetitive tasks. It is not “doing everything” in the abstract. It is doing almost everything a business needs in the space of lightweight, functional technology.

For SMBs, this matters because speed, clarity, and usefulness are often more valuable than complexity. CatchDog turns messy operational needs into systems, assets, and workflows that reduce friction and accelerate execution. It is a company designed for the AI era: not defined by one service category, but by the ability to keep adapting as the tools expand and the business problems become clearer.

title: You don't need to deal with technology
excerpt: Most companies don’t have an AI problem. They have operational friction: disconnected tools, manual steps, and systems that don’t work together. The worst outcome is using AI where human judgment is essential, while people keep wasting time on low-value repetitive tasks.
body:
Most businesses don’t wake up thinking they need AI.

They struggle with something much more concrete: too many tools, too many manual steps, too much time lost moving information from one place to another.

The problem is rarely “we need artificial intelligence.”

The problem is usually: this process is slow, this follow-up depends on memory, this information is duplicated, this tool does not talk to that tool, this client experience feels messy, this team is wasting time on work that should not require human attention.

That distinction matters.

Because the point is not to add AI everywhere. In fact, one of the worst mistakes a business can make is using AI where human judgment, trust, taste, or strategic thinking are essential.

The real opportunity is different: use technology to remove the operational weight that keeps people away from the work where they actually create value.

Most companies already have enough tools. Email, spreadsheets, forms, CRMs, calendars, cloud folders, messaging apps. What they usually lack is coherence.

When systems don’t communicate, people become the interface.

They copy, paste, check, remind, update, resend, rename, classify, chase, and follow up. That is where time is lost. That is where errors appear. That is where good teams become tired teams.

This is where AI can matter — not as a product label, but as part of a practical system.

A useful system can classify information, prioritize requests, trigger the right follow-up, route a lead, organize documents, draft a first response, or connect different tools into one operational flow.

The client does not need to deal with the technology behind it.

The client needs to explain the business problem clearly.

That is the kind of work I want to do with CatchDog: sit with a business owner, understand where the friction is, and build lightweight systems that make the operation easier, faster, and more coherent.

I have been working with AI as a collaborative layer since 2018, starting with research at AI Lab, University of Buenos Aires. Not as a tool to “prompt,” but as a way to extend thinking and build systems around it.

That is the foundation behind CatchDog LLC.

Most of the time, clients don’t ask for AI.

They ask for things to work.

And that is exactly the point.

title: From Tech Analysis to Building With AI
excerpt: For years, I studied, reported on, and explained technology. Generative AI changed something deeper: it gave people with strategic, humanistic, and analytical backgrounds the ability to build, not just interpret.
body:
For years, my work was to observe technology, understand it, explain it, and translate its impact for broader audiences.

As a journalist, I covered software, AI, Web3, startups, business models, and the way technology was reshaping economies in Latin America and the United States. I was not only reporting on tools or companies. I was trying to understand the social transformation behind them.

Artificial intelligence always felt different to me. Unlike other innovations that affect specific sectors, AI was clearly going to change the way society thinks, works, communicates, decides, and creates. That is why I followed it closely, both as a journalist and through academic and research work.

At the same time, since 2010, I have also built and led agencies in digital marketing and public relations. I wrote, designed strategies, advised clients, analyzed business models, and worked closely with technological change. In many ways, I became a technology humanist: someone who could understand technology not only as infrastructure, but as a multifactor phenomenon, which impacts culture, economy, communication, and human behavior.

But there was always a limitation.

Whenever I wanted to move from thinking to doing — from strategy to interface, from concept to prototype, from idea to system — I needed someone else to execute. A designer, a developer, an editor, a technician.

That dependency created friction.

Not because technical work does not matter. It matters enormously. But in many projects, the final decision-making power ended up in the hands of the people who knew how to build, even when they did not necessarily have the broader vision of what should be built, why it mattered, or how it should work for real people.

Generative AI changed that equation.

At first, it was overwhelming. It seemed like I had to absorb tasks that used to belong to other professionals. But as the tools improved, something shifted. I started learning faster. I started testing faster. I started building faster.

The distance between thinking and making became shorter.

That is the foundation behind CatchDog.

With an AI-driven mindset, I can now create not only content — text, images, video, scripts, explainers — but also functional systems: websites, dashboards, automations, lightweight apps, prototypes, and internal tools that actually work.

This does not mean that expertise disappears. It means that the center of gravity changes.

In many cases, generative AI lowers the barrier to execution. That can produce mediocre work when there is no strong judgment behind it. But for someone with years of experience analyzing technology, business, communication, and human behavior, it creates the opposite effect: it unlocks execution.

It allows the person with the vision to build.

That is why this moment feels liberating to me. Coming from journalism and the humanities is a huge advantage. It means I do not approach AI as a toy, a trend, a prompt trick, or just a complex tool. I approach it as a system of social, economic, and operational transformation. I have the main frame of it.

CatchDog exists because I no longer have to stop at analysis.

I can think, design, test, build, and deliver. 

And for small and mid-sized businesses, that matters. They do not always need a massive software project. They need someone who can understand the real problem, translate it into a practical digital solution, and build something useful without turning the process into an expensive, overcomplicated implementation.

That is the kind of work I want CatchDog to do.

Not technology for its own sake.

Not AI as decoration.

Technology shaped by judgment, strategy, and human understanding — and finally built by the same kind of mind that knows why it should exist.
